newsitem.title: USA: DOLLAR ENDS HIGHER AFTER BUBA LEAVES REPO STEADY.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR ENDS HIGHER AFTER BUBA LEAVES REPO STEADY.

text.p: Dollar/mark ended higher in quiet trade after the German central bank held market interest rates steady while dollar/yen benefited from short-covering.

The dollar jumped about half a pfennig overnight, before backing off in U.S. trade, after the Bundesbank's weekly money market operations, which fixed the key repo rate at 3.0 percent, where it has been for a year.

The bank set its rate for another week and refrained from preannouncing the following operation, rekindling fears that it might allow the market to set the repo higher next week upon its return from summer recess.
"It failed to stay up because the risk to switch to variable (rates) is still very much present," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics a Connecticut consulting firm.
The brief rally topped 1.87 marks, the dollar's best level since Friday's nerve-wracking slide dragged it almost 3.0 percent off a near-eight year high set early last week.
The dollar closed at 1.8625/35 marks, up a bit from 1.8610/20 at the open and at 116.23/33 yen, up from 115.80/90.
Intense speculation that higher German rates would be tolerated in order to curb the mark's steady decline this year had waned in recent days.
Many traders were starting to conclude Germany needed a weak currency to keep its exports and economy competitive before Europe lauches its single currency in 1999.
But although the outlook for German interest rates has clouded somewhat, many speculators remain in the dollar-bullish camp.

The strong U.S. economy and comparatively attractive interest rates are still working in favor of the dollar, and for many professionals a test of 1.90 marks, just above last week's peak, is just a matter of time.

"It's definitely cautious but I think we had a bit of a correction and you still have to look to buy on dips," said Lizbeth Goldberg, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank.
The dollar brushed above 116.50 yen, prompting a quick rush to cover earlier short sales. But the advance faltered withtraders expecting Japanese sell orders before 117 yen.
"Stop losses were run on the break of 116.50 yen, and that was the key to the move up," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
Any big move higher is not expected to come before data on U.S. July producer prices and retail sales is released on Wednesday, followed by consumer price figures on Thursday.

With price pressures apparently well contained, the market should zero in on the sales data. Analysts said these could be boosted by strong automobile sales and might fan fears that higher U.S. rates are possible to slow the economy.
"That should put the scare back in the bond market and I think dollar bulls probably want to see the bond market stabilize before they get aggressive about buying," Gilmore said.
After early gains, bonds and stocks ended down on Tuesday, with the Dow industrials falling 101 points to at 7961.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.5253/63 Swiss francs from 1.5245/55 and ended at Canadian $1.3934/39.
The pound fell to $1.5785/95 from $1.5845/55 and the Australian dollar fell to $0.7402/07 from $0.7412/17.
